introduction: On this Sunday, Jeremiah complains that speaking God's word has brought him only mockery, yet it burns like fire in his heart and he cannot hold it in. In the Gospel, after Peter's confession, Jesus speaks of his coming suffering; when Peter objects, Jesus calls us to deny ourselves, take up our cross and follow him. Paul urges us to offer ourselves as a living sacrifice. Let us follow Christ, whatever it costs.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, our souls thirst for God. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may not be conformed to this world but transformed by the renewal of her mind. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who suffer ridicule or rejection for speaking God's word: that God may strengthen them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who carry heavy crosses: that they may know that Jesus walks with them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who have gained much but lost their way: that they may find what truly matters. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may offer our bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, your Son calls us to take up our cross and follow him. Give us the courage to lose our lives for his sake, so that we may find them. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Take up your cross
reflection.body:
Jeremiah's words are some of the most honest in the Bible. He feels that God has overpowered him: "LORD, you have persuaded me, and I was persuaded." Speaking God's word has made him a laughingstock. He has tried to stop: "If I say that I will not make mention of him, or speak any more in his name, then there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones." He cannot keep silent. God's word burns within him.

In the Gospel, Peter has just confessed Jesus as the Christ. Now Jesus begins to explain that he "must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things... and be killed, and the third day be raised up." Peter is horrified and takes him aside: "Far be it from you, Lord! This will never be done to you." The rock of last week becomes a stumbling block. Jesus says, "Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men."

Then Jesus explains what following him means: "If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me." And he asks a question that cuts through all our ambitions: "For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his life?"

Paul tells us how to live this out: "present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God." And: "Don't be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind." The world pushes us to save ourselves; the Gospel invites us to give ourselves.

The psalm expresses the desire that makes this possible: "God, you are my God. I will earnestly seek you. My soul thirsts for you." This week, name the cross you are carrying, and carry it with Jesus. And ask where the world is shaping you more than the Gospel.
